questions.q: Define matter.
questions.a: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
wrong: Anything that is visible, including light
Anything that transfers energy, including sound

questions.q: Define an atom.
questions.a: The smallest particle of an element that retains that element's identity.
wrong: The smallest particle of a compound
A group of different elements mixed together

questions.q: Define an element.
questions.a: A substance made of only one type of atom.
wrong: A substance containing several types of atom bonded together
A substance made of different materials physically mixed

questions.q: Define a molecule.
questions.a: A group of atoms chemically bonded and acting as one particle.
wrong: A single atom with no bonds
A mixture of unbonded substances

questions.q: Define a compound.
questions.a: A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
wrong: Two or more elements mixed in any ratio
Two or more atoms of the same element bonded together

questions.q: Explain why O₂ is an element rather than a compound.
questions.a: It contains only one type of atom.
wrong: It has two different types of atom
Any particle with two atoms must be a compound

questions.q: State what a subscript in a formula shows.
questions.a: The number of atoms of the preceding element in one molecule or formula unit.
wrong: The number of molecules in the whole sample
The total number of different elements present

questions.q: Explain why NaCl is not described as a discrete molecule.
questions.a: It forms an extended ionic lattice; the formula shows the simplest ratio.
wrong: It contains only one type of atom
It consists of separate sodium chloride molecules

questions.q: Which two properties define matter?
questions.a: It has mass and takes up space.
wrong: It has colour and a fixed shape
It gives out light and transfers heat

questions.q: Name the tiny particles that make up all ordinary matter.
questions.a: Atoms
wrong: Cells
Molecules of water only

questions.q: State what sub-microscopic means when describing atoms.
questions.a: They are too small to see directly with an ordinary microscope.
wrong: They are large enough to see with the naked eye
They can always be seen with a school light microscope

questions.q: State whether the space between particles is completely filled with matter. Explain your answer.
questions.a: No. The particle model includes empty space between particles.
wrong: Yes. The gaps are always full of air particles
Yes. Matter completely fills every gap

questions.q: Describe the changes when a gas is compressed.
questions.a: The spacing between its particles decreases, not the particle size.
wrong: The individual particles shrink
The number of particles increases

questions.q: State what a solid particle diagram should show.
questions.a: Particles close together in a fixed arrangement
wrong: Particles far apart and free to move randomly
Particles close together and freely flowing past each other

questions.q: State what a liquid particle diagram should show.
questions.a: Particles close together with an irregular arrangement and able to move past one another
wrong: Particles fixed in a regular arrangement
Particles far apart with no attraction

questions.q: State what a gas particle diagram should show.
questions.a: Particles far apart and moving in different directions
wrong: Particles touching in fixed positions
Particles close together and sliding past each other

questions.q: Name the table that lists all known chemical elements.
questions.a: On the periodic table
wrong: On a food web
On a reactivity series only

questions.q: State what a chemical symbol identifies.
questions.a: An element
wrong: A whole mixture
A type of chemical reaction

questions.q: Describe how a two-letter element symbol is capitalised.
questions.a: The first letter is uppercase and the second is lowercase.
wrong: Both letters are uppercase
The first letter is lowercase and the second is uppercase

questions.q: Describe how a particle diagram can show a pure element.
questions.a: Every particle contains only the same type of atom.
wrong: Every particle has two different atom types
Several different unbonded particle types are present

questions.q: State whether a molecule of an element can contain two or more atoms. Explain your answer.
questions.a: Yes. An elemental molecule such as O₂ still contains only one atom type.
wrong: No. Two bonded atoms must always be different elements
No. An element must consist of isolated atoms

questions.q: Describe how a compound can be recognised in a particle diagram.
questions.a: Each compound particle contains two or more different atom types bonded in a fixed ratio.
wrong: All particles contain only one type of atom
Different atom types are present but never bonded

questions.q: State whether a molecule can be an element. Explain your answer.
questions.a: Yes, if all its atoms are the same element.
wrong: No. All molecules are compounds
No. Elements cannot form chemical bonds

questions.q: Explain why carbon dioxide is both a molecule and a compound.
questions.a: It is a bonded group containing atoms of two different elements.
wrong: It is a physical mixture of carbon and oxygen
It contains two atoms of the same element

questions.q: Define chemically bonded.
questions.a: Atoms are joined through a chemical interaction as part of the same particle or structure.
wrong: Atoms are simply touching with no chemical interaction
Atoms are separated by empty space and never interact

questions.q: State what a fixed ratio means in a compound.
questions.a: The elements occur in the same numerical proportion in that compound.
wrong: The amount of each element can vary freely
Every compound contains equal numbers of each atom type

questions.q: State what a chemical formula tells you about the elements in a substance.
questions.a: Which elements are present in the substance
wrong: The exact temperature of the substance
The colour and state of the substance

questions.q: State the number of atoms represented by an element symbol with no subscript in a chemical formula.
questions.a: One
wrong: Zero
Two

questions.q: State how many hydrogen atoms are represented in H₂O.
questions.a: Two
wrong: One
Three

questions.q: State how many oxygen atoms are represented in H₂O.
questions.a: One
wrong: Two
Three

questions.q: State what brackets mean in a chemical formula.
questions.a: The group inside the brackets is treated together and multiplied by the following subscript.
wrong: The group inside is added only once regardless of the subscript
Only the first element inside is multiplied

questions.q: State what a coefficient in front of a formula multiplies.
questions.a: The whole formula
wrong: Only the final element in the formula
Only the first element in the formula

questions.q: Explain why NaCl represents a ratio rather than one molecule.
questions.a: Sodium chloride forms a repeating ionic lattice.
wrong: It consists of isolated NaCl molecules
Sodium and chlorine are mixed in a variable ratio

questions.q: Define a scientific model.
questions.a: A simplified representation used to explain, predict or communicate an idea
wrong: A perfect full-sized copy containing every detail
A guess that cannot be checked against evidence

questions.q: Explain why a formula might be a useful model.
questions.a: It communicates which elements are present and their numerical proportions.
wrong: It shows the exact three-dimensional shape of every substance
It shows only the substance's colour

questions.q: Explain why a particle diagram might be a useful model.
questions.a: It can represent particle types, spacing, arrangement and bonding.
wrong: It shows atoms at their actual size on the page
It proves that particles have the colours used in the drawing

questions.q: Explain why a model is not a perfect copy of a substance.
questions.a: It simplifies selected features and leaves other features out.
wrong: It includes every detail at exactly the correct scale
The simplified features can never be used to make predictions

questions.q: Describe how a pure substance appears in a particle diagram.
questions.a: Only one type of particle is present.
wrong: Several different particle types are present
Every particle must contain only one atom

questions.q: Describe how a mixture appears in a particle diagram.
questions.a: More than one type of particle is present and the substances are not bonded into a new substance.
wrong: Only one type of particle is present
All components are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio

questions.q: State whether a sample that looks uniform can still be a mixture. Explain your answer.
questions.a: Yes. Air and salt water are mixtures even though they can look uniform.
wrong: No. Every mixture must have visible layers
No. A uniform appearance proves that a substance is pure

questions.q: Name the vertical columns of the periodic table.
questions.a: Groups
wrong: Periods
Rows

questions.q: Name the horizontal rows of the periodic table.
questions.a: Periods
wrong: Groups
Families

questions.q: State one piece of information shown in an element's periodic-table box.
questions.a: Its element symbol or atomic number
wrong: Its current room temperature
Its price per kilogram

questions.q: Describe how Group 17 reactivity changes down the group.
questions.a: It decreases.
wrong: It increases
It stays the same for every element

questions.q: State where most metals are found on the periodic table.
questions.a: On the left and in the centre.
wrong: Only on the far right
Only in the top row

questions.q: Describe how Group 1 reactivity changes down the group.
questions.a: It increases.
wrong: It decreases
It stays the same for every element

questions.q: Identify which group contains the noble gases.
questions.a: Group 18
wrong: Group 1
Group 17

questions.q: Explain why Mendeleev left gaps in his table.
questions.a: He predicted that undiscovered elements would fill them and have particular properties.
wrong: He had no way to predict properties of missing elements
He wanted every group to have only three elements

questions.q: Explain why elements are arranged in a periodic table.
questions.a: The arrangement reveals repeating patterns in their physical and chemical properties.
wrong: It arranges elements by their colour only
It places all elements in alphabetical order

questions.q: State what elements in one vertical group tend to share.
questions.a: Similar chemical properties
wrong: The same atomic number
Exactly the same mass

questions.q: Name the scientist who developed an early periodic table that successfully predicted missing elements.
questions.a: Dmitri Mendeleev
wrong: Isaac Newton
Charles Darwin

questions.q: Explain why Mendeleev's gaps were scientifically useful.
questions.a: They allowed him to predict the properties of elements that had not yet been discovered.
wrong: They showed that no more elements could exist
They proved that atomic numbers were all identical

questions.q: Describe how the periodic table can be used as a scientific model.
questions.a: Position and patterns help classify elements and predict properties.
wrong: It shows the actual size of every atom
It lists elements randomly without useful patterns

questions.q: Describe how elements are broadly classified.
questions.a: As metals or non-metals
wrong: As acids or alkalis only
As organisms or minerals only

questions.q: State one physical property commonly shown by metals.
questions.a: For example, lustre, malleability, ductility, high conductivity or a relatively high melting point
wrong: Poor electrical conductivity
Brittleness and no lustre in all cases

questions.q: State one physical property commonly shown by non-metals.
questions.a: For example, low conductivity, a lower boiling point or being a gas at room temperature
wrong: High electrical conductivity
Easy drawing into metal wires

questions.q: Explain why metals are often used for electrical wiring.
questions.a: Many metals conduct electricity and can be drawn into wires.
wrong: They prevent electrical current from flowing
They are all liquid at room temperature

questions.q: Identify which name is given to the Group 1 elements.
questions.a: Alkali metals
wrong: Noble gases
Halogens

questions.q: Name one Group 1 element.
questions.a: Lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium or caesium
wrong: Chlorine
Calcium

questions.q: Explain why Group 1 metals are stored under oil.
questions.a: They are very reactive, so the oil limits contact with air and water.
wrong: Oil makes them completely unreactive forever
Oil increases their contact with water

questions.q: Describe how the reaction with water changes from lithium to sodium to potassium.
questions.a: It becomes more vigorous down the group.
wrong: It becomes less vigorous down the group
All three react at exactly the same rate

questions.q: Identify which gas forms when a Group 1 metal reacts with water.
questions.a: Hydrogen
wrong: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide

questions.q: Identify which type of compound forms when a Group 1 metal reacts with water.
questions.a: A metal hydroxide
wrong: A metal carbonate
A metal chloride

questions.q: State one physical property common to Group 1 metals.
questions.a: They are soft, low-density metals with relatively low melting points.
wrong: They are all very hard with extremely high melting points
They are all gases at room temperature

questions.q: Identify which name is given to the Group 2 elements.
questions.a: Alkaline earth metals
wrong: Alkali metals
Halogens

questions.q: Compare the reactivity of Group 2 and Group 1 metals in the same period.
questions.a: Group 2 metals are reactive but less reactive than Group 1 metals.
wrong: Group 2 metals are always more reactive
Both groups have exactly the same reactivity

questions.q: Describe how reactivity changes down Group 2.
questions.a: It increases.
wrong: It decreases
It stays the same

questions.q: Identify which reacts more vigorously with hydrochloric acid: magnesium or calcium.
questions.a: Calcium, because it is lower in Group 2.
wrong: Magnesium, because it is higher in Group 2
Both always react at the same rate

questions.q: State the products when a Group 2 metal reacts with an acid.
questions.a: A salt and hydrogen gas
wrong: A salt and oxygen gas
A salt and carbon dioxide gas

questions.q: Describe a positive test result for hydrogen gas.
questions.a: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop.
wrong: A glowing splint relights
Limewater turns cloudy

questions.q: Identify which name is given to the Group 17 elements.
questions.a: Halogens
wrong: Noble gases
Alkaline earth metals

questions.q: Name one halogen.
questions.a: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine or iodine
wrong: Sodium
Argon

questions.q: Describe how reactivity changes down Group 17.
questions.a: It decreases.
wrong: It increases
It stays the same

questions.q: Describe how the reactivity of Group 17 elements changes down the periodic table.
questions.a: A halogen higher up Group 17 is more reactive than one lower down.
wrong: A halogen lower down is more reactive
Every halogen has the same reactivity

questions.q: Give one use of a Group 17 element (halogen).
questions.a: For example, chlorine is used to disinfect water or iodine is used as an antiseptic.
wrong: Helium in a balloon
Copper in electrical wiring

questions.q: Describe what happens when iodine is warmed.
questions.a: It forms a purple vapour.
wrong: It forms a green vapour
It turns into a magnetic metal

questions.q: What name is given to Group 18 elements?
questions.a: Noble gases
wrong: Halogens
Alkali metals

questions.q: Explain why noble gases are used in balloons, signs or welding.
questions.a: They are non-reactive under normal conditions, so they are useful when reactions are unwanted.
wrong: They react rapidly with other materials
They are all highly flammable

questions.q: Define a phenotype.
questions.a: The observable characteristics or traits of an organism.
wrong: Only the genetic information an organism inherits
Only the environment surrounding an organism

questions.q: Which two broad influences shape phenotype?
questions.a: Genes and the environment
wrong: Genes and chance alone, with no environmental influence
Environment alone, with no genetic influence

questions.q: Define a gene.
questions.a: A section of DNA containing instructions for making a protein or part of a protein.
wrong: A whole cell containing many nuclei
A protein containing instructions for making DNA

questions.q: Describe how genes influence traits.
questions.a: Genes provide instructions for proteins that affect structures and cell functions.
wrong: Genes directly change every trait without involving proteins
Genes affect traits only after the organism dies

questions.q: Define gene expression.
questions.a: The activity of a gene that results in its product being made.
wrong: A gene moving from the nucleus into another organism
A gene disappearing whenever its product is made

questions.q: Give one environmental factor that can influence trait expression.
questions.a: For example, nutrition, temperature, light or soil pH.
wrong: The chemical symbol for an element
The atomic number of a metal

questions.q: Explain why 'one gene for each whole trait' is often inaccurate.
questions.a: Most traits are influenced by many genes and environmental factors.
wrong: Each whole trait is always controlled by exactly one gene
Environmental factors never affect traits

questions.q: State what a fair investigation of an environmental signal should identify.
questions.a: An independent variable, dependent variable, control variables and repeats.
wrong: Only the desired result and no measured variables
Several variables to change together without controls

questions.q: Define an observable trait.
questions.a: A characteristic that can be seen or measured
wrong: A section of DNA that is never expressed
Only a characteristic that cannot be measured

questions.q: Explain why two organisms with similar inherited information can show different traits.
questions.a: Environmental conditions can affect how traits develop or are expressed.
wrong: Identical inherited information guarantees identical traits in every environment
Environmental conditions replace all inherited DNA

questions.q: State where most DNA is found in a plant or animal cell.
questions.a: In chromosomes in the nucleus
wrong: In the cell membrane
Dissolved freely in the cytoplasm only

questions.q: Define a chromosome.
questions.a: A structure made of DNA that carries many genes
wrong: A protein that contains no DNA
A single atom found in the nucleus

questions.q: Describe how nucleus, chromosome, DNA and gene are related.
questions.a: The nucleus contains chromosomes; chromosomes are made of DNA; genes are sections of DNA.
wrong: Genes contain nuclei, and nuclei are made of chromosomes
Chromosomes contain cells, and DNA is made of nuclei

questions.q: State what a gene contains instructions for making.
questions.a: Instructions for making a protein or part of a protein
wrong: Instructions for making a whole ecosystem
Instructions for making individual atoms

questions.q: Describe how a protein can affect an observable trait.
questions.a: Proteins influence cell structures and processes that contribute to the trait.
wrong: Proteins have no effect on cell processes
Proteins influence traits only by changing the weather

questions.q: State whether every trait is controlled by a single gene. Explain your answer.
questions.a: No. Most traits are influenced by many genes and the environment.
wrong: Yes. Every trait has exactly one controlling gene
Yes. Environmental factors cannot influence any trait

questions.q: State what the information in an active gene is used to produce.
questions.a: Its information is being used to make its product.
wrong: Its information is destroyed instead of used
Its information automatically leaves the organism

questions.q: Describe how soil pH can affect hydrangea flower colour.
questions.a: Soil conditions can influence processes and gene activity involved in producing flower pigments.
wrong: Soil pH paints pigments directly onto the petals
Soil pH cannot influence flower colour

questions.q: Describe how temperature can affect traits in some organisms.
questions.a: Temperature can act as an environmental signal during development.
wrong: Temperature cannot affect development or traits
Temperature changes every inherited gene into a new gene

questions.q: Describe how nutrition can influence phenotype.
questions.a: Nutrient availability can affect growth, development and the activity of cell processes.
wrong: Nutrition affects only the environment and never the organism
Nutrients replace every inherited gene

questions.q: Explain why phenotype should not be described as caused only by DNA.
questions.a: Many phenotypes result from interactions between genetic information and the environment.
wrong: All phenotypes depend only on DNA
The environment has no role in phenotype

questions.q: Define inherited variation.
questions.a: Differences linked to genetic information received from parents
wrong: Differences caused only by diet after birth
Differences caused only by temperature during development

questions.q: Define environmental variation.
questions.a: Differences produced by conditions or experiences in the environment
wrong: Differences caused only by genes received from parents
Differences that cannot be influenced by surroundings

questions.q: Define the independent variable in an investigation.
questions.a: The factor deliberately changed
wrong: The outcome that is measured
A factor deliberately kept constant

questions.q: Define the dependent variable in an investigation.
questions.a: The outcome measured or observed
wrong: The factor deliberately changed
A factor deliberately kept constant

questions.q: Define control variables.
questions.a: Factors kept the same so the test is fair
wrong: Factors deliberately changed in every trial
Outcomes measured to see what happened

questions.q: Explain why repeats are needed in an investigation of environmental effects.
questions.a: They show variation and improve confidence that a pattern is reliable.
wrong: They guarantee that all results will be identical
They remove every systematic error automatically

questions.q: Explain why an investigation should use an appropriate range of environmental conditions.
questions.a: A suitable range makes it possible to detect and describe a trend.
wrong: Only one environmental condition is enough to show any trend
A range prevents any changes being detected

questions.q: State what a results table should contain.
questions.a: Clearly labelled variables, units where needed, and recorded repeat measurements or observations
wrong: Unlabelled values without units or repeats
Only the conclusion, without measured values

questions.q: Define a trend in data.
questions.a: A consistent pattern or relationship between variables
wrong: A single unusual result far from the others
A prediction made before any results are collected

questions.q: Explain why a conclusion must refer to data.
questions.a: The data are the evidence for the claimed effect on the trait.
wrong: The conclusion is evidence even if the data disagree
Data are useful only if they match the prediction

questions.q: Define continuous variation.
questions.a: Variation that can take any value across a range
wrong: Variation that can fall only into separate categories
Variation found only in organisms with identical traits

questions.q: Give one example of a continuously varying trait.
questions.a: For example, height or mass
wrong: ABO blood group
Presence or absence of a genetic condition

questions.q: Define discontinuous variation.
questions.a: Variation that falls into separate categories
wrong: Variation that takes every possible value in a range
Variation caused only by measurement error

questions.q: Identify which graph is suitable for separate trait categories.
questions.a: A bar chart
wrong: A line graph joining category names in order
A scatter graph with arbitrary numerical codes for categories

questions.q: Identify which graph is suitable for continuous measurements grouped into intervals.
questions.a: A histogram
wrong: A pie chart of every individual measurement
A bar chart with gaps between adjacent numerical intervals

questions.q: Explain why a model linking genes, proteins and environment is useful.
questions.a: It shows how several influences can combine to produce a phenotype.
wrong: It proves that one gene controls every whole trait
It removes the need to consider environmental influences

questions.q: State one limitation of a simple trait model.
questions.a: It may make a multi-gene, environmentally influenced trait look simpler than it really is.
wrong: It includes every influence and has no limitations
It proves environmental conditions are irrelevant

questions.q: Name the starting substances in a reaction.
questions.a: Reactants
wrong: Products
Catalysts only

questions.q: Name the substances formed.
questions.a: Products
wrong: Reactants
Indicators only

questions.q: State what the arrow in a chemical equation means.
questions.a: Reacts to form
wrong: Is physically mixed with
Has exactly the same properties as

questions.q: State the condition that makes a chemical equation balanced.
questions.a: When each type of atom has the same total number on both sides.
wrong: When both sides have the same number of molecules only
When every coefficient is the same

questions.q: Explain why subscripts must not be changed when balancing a chemical equation.
questions.a: Changing a subscript changes the identity of the substance.
wrong: Subscripts can always be changed without affecting substances
Subscripts change only the temperature of the reaction

questions.q: Define an exothermic reaction.
questions.a: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings.
wrong: A reaction that takes energy from the surroundings
A reaction that never transfers energy

questions.q: State the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide and water
wrong: Carbon monoxide and hydrogen only
Carbon and oxygen only

questions.q: Describe what occurs in a displacement reaction.
questions.a: A more reactive metal replaces a less reactive metal in a compound.
wrong: A less reactive metal always replaces a more reactive one
Any two metals exchange places regardless of reactivity

questions.q: Name one observation that can provide evidence of a chemical reaction.
questions.a: For example, gas formation, a precipitate, temperature change or colour change
wrong: Only a change of container
Only a change in position of the beaker

questions.q: Explain why gas bubbles can be evidence of a reaction.
questions.a: A new gas substance may be forming.
wrong: Bubbles prove that atoms are being destroyed
Bubbles always mean a liquid is freezing

questions.q: Define a precipitate.
questions.a: A new insoluble solid formed during a reaction
wrong: A gas released by heating a liquid
A substance that dissolves completely during mixing

questions.q: Explain why a temperature change can be evidence of a chemical reaction.
questions.a: Energy may be transferred as new substances form.
wrong: Atoms gain mass whenever the temperature rises
Temperature changes prove no new substances have formed

questions.q: Define a reactant.
questions.a: A starting substance in a chemical reaction
wrong: A substance formed at the end of a reaction
A substance that can never change chemically

questions.q: Define a product.
questions.a: A new substance formed in a chemical reaction
wrong: A starting substance that is used in a reaction
Only an insoluble solid formed in a reaction

questions.q: State what a word equation communicates.
questions.a: The names of the reactants and products in a reaction
wrong: Only the colours of the substances
Only the masses of the containers

questions.q: Describe how the arrow in a word equation can be read aloud.
questions.a: Reacts to form
wrong: Is identical to
Has the same number of molecules as

questions.q: State where reactants are written in a chemical equation.
questions.a: On the left of the arrow
wrong: On the right of the arrow
Always above the arrow

questions.q: State where products are written in a chemical equation.
questions.a: On the right of the arrow
wrong: On the left of the arrow
Always below the arrow

questions.q: State what must be equal on both sides of a balanced chemical equation.
questions.a: The number of atoms of each element
wrong: The number of molecules regardless of atom types
The number of reactants and products listed

questions.q: Identify which number can be changed to balance an equation.
questions.a: A coefficient in front of a formula
wrong: A subscript within a formula
An element's atomic number

questions.q: Explain why changing a subscript is incorrect when balancing a chemical equation.
questions.a: It changes the identity or formula of the substance.
wrong: It changes only the size of the written text
It changes only the number of molecules, never their identity

questions.q: Describe how an equation should be checked after coefficients are added.
questions.a: Count the atoms of every element on both sides again.
wrong: Check only that both sides have the same number of letters
Count only one chosen element and ignore the others

questions.q: Describe how a balanced equation represents conservation of atoms.
questions.a: It shows that the same number of each type of atom is present before and after the reaction.
wrong: Atoms disappear and new atom types are created
Every reactant molecule survives unchanged

questions.q: State what the pH scale tells us about an aqueous solution.
questions.a: Whether a solution is acidic, neutral or alkaline
wrong: The mass of dissolved material only
The electrical conductivity only

questions.q: State what an indicator can show.
questions.a: A colour that gives evidence about a solution's pH range
wrong: The exact identity of every dissolved substance
The total number of molecules in the solution

questions.q: Identify which pH is neutral.
Identify which pH values are acidic.
questions.a: Below 7
wrong: Above 7
Exactly 7

questions.q: Identify which pH values are alkaline.
questions.a: Above 7
wrong: Below 7
Exactly 7

questions.q: State the products of neutralisation between an acid and a base.
questions.a: A salt and water
wrong: A salt and hydrogen
A salt and carbon dioxide

questions.q: Identify which gas forms when a suitable metal reacts with an acid.
questions.a: Hydrogen
wrong: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide

questions.q: Identify which gas forms when an acid reacts with a carbonate.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide
wrong: Hydrogen
Oxygen

questions.q: Describe what happens to the surroundings during an exothermic reaction.
questions.a: They gain energy and usually warm up.
wrong: They lose energy and usually cool down
Their energy and temperature must stay unchanged

questions.q: Describe what happens to the surroundings during an endothermic reaction.
questions.a: They lose energy and usually cool down.
wrong: They gain energy and usually warm up
They must give out light without any energy transfer

questions.q: A reaction mixture warms its surroundings. Classify the reaction as exothermic or endothermic.
questions.a: Exothermic
wrong: Endothermic
Neither: no energy transfer occurs

questions.q: A reaction mixture cools its surroundings. Classify the reaction as exothermic or endothermic.
questions.a: Endothermic
wrong: Exothermic
Neither: cooling means no energy transfer

questions.q: Name the two reactants required for combustion.
questions.a: A fuel and oxygen
wrong: A fuel and nitrogen
Carbon dioxide and water

questions.q: Identify which energy changes are commonly observed in combustion.
questions.a: Heat and light are released.
wrong: Heat and light are absorbed from the surroundings
No energy is transferred to the surroundings

questions.q: Identify which forms during complete combustion of a hydrocarbon.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide and water
wrong: Carbon monoxide and hydrogen only
A salt and water only

questions.q: State when one metal can displace another from a compound solution.
questions.a: When the added metal is more reactive than the metal in the compound.
wrong: When the added metal is less reactive
Whenever the two metals have different colours

questions.q: Describe how a displacement reaction can compare metal reactivity.
questions.a: If one metal replaces another, the added metal is more reactive.
wrong: The replaced metal is always more reactive
Any metal that dissolves must be less reactive

questions.q: State the SI unit of force.
questions.a: Newton (N)
wrong: Kilogram (kg)
Pascal (Pa)

questions.q: State what the direction and length of a force arrow represent.
questions.a: The direction and relative magnitude of the force.
wrong: The object's speed and mass
The object's acceleration and temperature

questions.q: Define net force.
questions.a: The overall force after all forces and directions are combined.
wrong: The largest force only, ignoring the others
The sum of force magnitudes with directions ignored

questions.q: Describe what happens when the net force is zero.
questions.a: An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity in a straight line.
wrong: It must slow down until it stops
It must accelerate in its current direction

questions.q: Define inertia.
questions.a: An object's resistance to a change in its motion.
wrong: The force that always slows a moving object
An object's ability to create energy

questions.q: Describe how mass affects inertia.
questions.a: Greater mass means greater inertia.
wrong: Greater mass means less inertia
Mass has no effect on inertia

questions.q: State Newton's Second Law equation.
questions.a: F = ma
wrong: F = m/a

questions.a: Predation, competition, food or disease can change survival and reproduction.
wrong: Biotic interactions cannot affect survival
Predation always increases the abundance of the prey

questions.q: State whether ecosystems are normally in a perfectly static balance. Explain your answer.
questions.a: No. They change through interactions and disturbances.
wrong: Yes. Population sizes never change naturally
Yes. Every disturbance permanently destroys all life

questions.q: Define a nutrient cycle.
questions.a: Movement and recycling of nutrients through organisms and the environment.
wrong: One-way movement of energy with no recycling of nutrients
Creation of new atoms by organisms

questions.q: Name three important cycles in ecosystems.
questions.a: Carbon, nitrogen and water cycles
wrong: Food, sunlight and sound cycles
Predator, prey and competition cycles

questions.q: Define decomposition.
questions.a: Breakdown of dead material and waste.
wrong: Production of food by photosynthesis
Movement of water vapour from plant leaves

questions.q: Explain why microorganisms are important in decomposition.
questions.a: They break down organic material and release nutrients for reuse.
wrong: They destroy all nutrients so none can be reused
They convert all dead material directly into sunlight

questions.q: State whether matter is used up in an ecosystem. Explain your answer.
questions.a: No. Matter is transferred and recycled.
wrong: Yes. Organisms permanently destroy atoms when they respire
Yes. Matter leaves existence after decomposition

questions.q: Define a carbon store.
questions.a: A part of the Earth system where carbon remains for a period, such as forests, soil or oceans.
wrong: A process that creates new carbon atoms
Only carbon dioxide currently moving through the atmosphere

questions.q: Describe how healthy soil can depend on decomposition.
questions.a: Decomposition returns mineral nutrients and organic matter to soil.
wrong: Decomposition removes all minerals from the soil forever
Decomposition prevents any organic matter entering soil

questions.q: State what a quadrat can help estimate about organisms in a habitat.
questions.a: The abundance or distribution of organisms in a defined area.
wrong: The exact age of every organism
The speed of all flying animals

questions.q: State the purpose of a transect in an ecological investigation.
questions.a: Sampling changes in organisms or conditions along a line.
wrong: Measuring only one chosen individual repeatedly
Collecting organisms only from the richest patch

questions.q: Explain why quadrats should be placed using an appropriate sampling method.
questions.a: To reduce bias and make the sample more representative.
wrong: To guarantee the highest possible organism count
To avoid ever sampling any unusual areas

questions.q: Describe how mean abundance can be calculated.
questions.a: Add the counts from samples and divide by the number of samples.
wrong: Multiply the highest count by the number of samples
Subtract the lowest count from the highest count

questions.q: Explain why multiple samples are needed.
questions.a: Organisms are unevenly distributed, so repeats improve representativeness and reliability.
wrong: One sample always represents every part of a habitat
Repeats make environmental differences disappear

questions.q: State whether quadrats can be used only for plants. Explain your answer.
questions.a: No. They can sample stationary or slow-moving organisms and traces.
wrong: Yes. No animals can ever be sampled with quadrats
Yes. Quadrats can measure only tree height

questions.q: Define ngā tohu o te taiao.
questions.a: Environmental signs or indicators used to understand seasonal change and ecosystem health.
wrong: A laboratory equation for pressure
A list of chemical symbols for minerals

questions.q: Describe how flowering or bird movement can act as an environmental indicator.
questions.a: Changes in timing or abundance can signal seasonal or ecosystem changes.
wrong: These changes never provide information about ecosystems
Only laboratory measurements can act as evidence

questions.q: State whether mātauranga Māori environmental knowledge is based on evidence. Explain your answer.
questions.a: It is based on sustained observation, experience and knowledge passed between generations.
wrong: No. It excludes observation of environmental patterns
No. It consists only of random predictions

questions.q: Define ecosystem stability.
questions.a: The capacity of a system to maintain or recover its functions through change.
wrong: The absence of every natural change
A guarantee that no population will ever change

questions.q: Define a disturbance in an ecosystem.
questions.a: An event or change that alters ecosystem structure or conditions.
wrong: An event that cannot affect living organisms
The total number of species in a habitat

questions.q: Give one example of an ecosystem disturbance.
questions.a: A new predator, drought, flood, disease, logging or pollution
wrong: Counting organisms without changing their habitat
Recording the temperature without changing it

questions.q: Explain why a new predator can affect more than its direct prey.
questions.a: Food-web relationships create indirect effects across multiple populations.
wrong: Only the prey can ever be affected
Food webs prevent indirect effects between populations

questions.q: Define interdependence.
questions.a: Organisms and environmental factors depend on and influence one another.
wrong: Each organism survives independently of its surroundings
Only predators depend on other organisms

questions.q: Define ecological restoration.
questions.a: Actions intended to repair ecosystem structure, function or biodiversity.
wrong: Replacing every habitat with a single introduced species
Removing all living organisms from a site

questions.q: Name one restoration strategy.
questions.a: Native planting, pest control, wetland restoration, pollution reduction or habitat protection
wrong: Introducing a new invasive predator
Increasing untreated pollution entering a river

questions.q: Define conservation.
questions.a: Protection and careful management of species, habitats and resources.
wrong: Using all available resources as quickly as possible
Replacing all native habitats with roads

questions.q: Define sustainability.
questions.a: Meeting needs while maintaining environmental systems for the future.
wrong: Meeting today's needs while ignoring future impacts
Using resources faster than natural systems can recover

questions.q: Explain why an ecosystem action plan should use evidence.
questions.a: Evidence helps identify causes, evaluate options and monitor whether actions work.
wrong: Evidence is useful only if it agrees with the preferred action
An action plan should never be changed after it begins

questions.q: Describe how local Waikato River data can support ecosystem decisions.
questions.a: It can reveal trends in water quality, species, land use and restoration outcomes.
wrong: Local data cannot show changes over time
Only data from unrelated rivers can inform local decisions

questions.q: Define directional hypothesis in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A prediction that states how the dependent variable will change
wrong: A summary written only after the results are collected
A list of hazards with no predicted relationship

questions.q: Name the term for “a prediction that states how the dependent variable will change”.
questions.a: directional hypothesis
wrong: method evaluation
controlled condition

questions.q: Explain why directional hypothesis matters in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: It gives a precise relationship that the results can support or challenge
wrong: It guarantees that the prediction will be correct
It removes the need to collect any data

questions.q: Define operational variable in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A variable defined by exactly how it will be changed or measured
wrong: A factor named without saying how it is measured
A result chosen after the conclusion is written

questions.q: Name the term for “a variable defined by exactly how it will be changed or measured”.
questions.a: operational variable
wrong: measurement uncertainty
directional hypothesis

questions.q: Explain why variables need to be defined in terms of how they are changed or measured.
questions.a: It makes the method clear enough for another person to repeat
wrong: It prevents anyone else from repeating the investigation
It means units and measurement methods are unnecessary

questions.q: Define controlled condition in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: An environmental or procedural factor kept constant across trials
wrong: The outcome deliberately measured in each trial
The factor deliberately changed between trials

questions.q: Name the term for “an environmental or procedural factor kept constant across trials”.
questions.a: controlled condition
wrong: random error
operational variable

questions.q: Explain why controlled condition matters in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: It prevents a confounding explanation for the observed pattern
wrong: It makes all variables change at the same time
It guarantees that every measurement has zero error

questions.q: Define instrument resolution in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: The smallest change that a measuring instrument can display
wrong: The largest value the instrument can measure
How close repeated readings are to one another

questions.q: Name the term for “the smallest change that a measuring instrument can display”.
questions.a: instrument resolution
wrong: measurement accuracy
measurement precision

questions.q: Explain why instrument resolution matters in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: Finer resolution allows smaller differences to be detected
wrong: It automatically removes all systematic errors
It guarantees every reading equals the true value

questions.q: Define random error in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: Unpredictable variation that makes repeated readings scatter
wrong: A consistent shift of every reading in one direction
A prediction about how the variables are related

questions.q: Name the term for “unpredictable variation that makes repeated readings scatter”.
questions.a: random error
wrong: systematic error
controlled condition

questions.q: Explain how repeating measurements and calculating a mean reduce the effect of random error.
questions.a: Repeats and a mean reduce its effect on the final value
wrong: A mean guarantees the exact true value
Repeating a reading makes its random error identical every time

questions.q: Define systematic error in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A consistent bias that shifts measurements in the same direction
wrong: Unpredictable scatter in repeated readings
The smallest change a scale can display

questions.q: Name the term for “a consistent bias that shifts measurements in the same direction”.
questions.a: systematic error
wrong: random error
measurement precision

questions.q: Explain why repeating readings cannot remove a systematic error.
questions.a: Repeating readings does not remove it, so the method or instrument must be corrected
wrong: Averaging enough repeats always cancels the fixed bias
Repeating readings turns a fixed bias into a true value

questions.q: Define zero error in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A non-zero instrument reading when the true value should be zero
wrong: An instrument showing zero when the true value is zero
Any scatter between repeated measurements

questions.q: Name the term for “a non-zero instrument reading when the true value should be zero”.
questions.a: zero error
wrong: random error
instrument resolution

questions.q: Explain why an instrument should be checked for zero error before measurements are taken.
questions.a: Checking and correcting the zero prevents a systematic offset
wrong: It increases the smallest scale division
It guarantees that random variation is impossible

questions.q: Define measurement accuracy in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: Closeness of a result to the accepted or true value
wrong: Closeness of repeated readings to each other
The smallest change an instrument can display

questions.q: Name the term for “closeness of a result to the accepted or true value”.
questions.a: measurement accuracy
wrong: measurement precision
instrument resolution

questions.q: Describe how calibration and reducing systematic errors can improve measurement accuracy.
questions.a: Calibration and suitable technique improve accuracy
wrong: Writing extra decimal places always improves accuracy
Repeating a biased method guarantees an accurate mean

questions.q: Define measurement precision in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: Closeness of repeated measurements to one another
wrong: Closeness to the accepted or true value
The largest value an instrument can display

questions.q: Name the term for “closeness of repeated measurements to one another”.
questions.a: measurement precision
wrong: measurement accuracy
measurement uncertainty

questions.q: Explain why precision and accuracy must be judged separately.
questions.a: Small spread indicates precise measurement but does not guarantee accuracy
wrong: Precise readings must always equal the true value
Accurate readings must always have zero spread

questions.q: Define repeatability in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: Agreement when the same person repeats a method using the same equipment
wrong: Agreement between different investigators using different methods
Agreement of a result with the true value

questions.q: Name the term for “agreement when the same person repeats a method using the same equipment”.
questions.a: repeatability
wrong: reproducibility
measurement accuracy

questions.q: Explain why repeatability matters in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: It tests whether the procedure gives consistent outcomes
wrong: It proves the result is accurate without any calibration
It removes all uncertainty from the measurements

questions.q: Define reproducibility in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: Agreement when a different person or method repeats the investigation
wrong: Agreement when only the same person uses the same equipment
The number of decimal places in a measurement

questions.q: Name the term for “agreement when a different person or method repeats the investigation”.
questions.a: reproducibility
wrong: repeatability
instrument resolution

questions.q: Explain why reproducibility matters in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: It provides a stronger check that the finding is not tied to one setup
wrong: It proves that every instrument has zero error
It replaces the need to describe the method

questions.q: Define measurement uncertainty in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: An estimated interval around a measured value within which the true value may lie
wrong: The exact error known with complete certainty
Only the largest reading in a set

questions.q: Name the term for “an estimated interval around a measured value within which the true value may lie”.
questions.a: measurement uncertainty
wrong: instrument resolution
measurement precision

questions.q: Explain why measurement uncertainty must be recorded and included in relevant calculations.
questions.a: It prevents measurements being reported with unjustified certainty
wrong: It makes a measured value exact
It removes the need to state measurement units

questions.q: Define significant figures in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: Digits used to show the precision justified by a measurement
wrong: Every digit displayed by a calculator, regardless of the data
Only the zeros before the first non-zero digit

questions.q: Name the term for “digits used to show the precision justified by a measurement”.
questions.a: significant figures
wrong: instrument resolution
zero error

questions.q: Explain why a calculated answer should not imply greater precision than the measurements used.
questions.a: Calculated answers should not imply greater precision than the data
wrong: More calculator digits always mean better measurements
Every calculated answer must contain ten decimal places

questions.q: Define scatter graph in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A graph of paired numerical data used to look for association
wrong: A graph showing only separate named categories
A graph showing parts of a whole as sectors

questions.q: Name the term for “a graph of paired numerical data used to look for association”.
questions.a: scatter graph
wrong: bar chart
pie chart

questions.q: Explain why scatter graph matters in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: It shows the direction, strength and shape of a possible relationship
wrong: It proves that one variable causes the other
It removes the need to inspect unusual points

questions.q: Define line of best fit in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A line positioned to represent the central trend through scattered points
wrong: A line joining every data point in order
A line forced through the origin in every investigation

questions.q: Name the term for “a line positioned to represent the central trend through scattered points”.
questions.a: line of best fit
wrong: line graph joining every point
risk matrix

questions.q: Explain why line of best fit matters in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: It supports estimates and gradient calculations without following noise
wrong: It must pass through every measurement
It proves every point away from the line is wrong

questions.q: Define correlation in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: An association in which two measured variables change together
wrong: Proof that one factor causes another
The amount by which an instrument fails to read zero

questions.q: Name the term for “an association in which two measured variables change together”.
questions.a: correlation
wrong: causal claim
zero error

questions.q: Explain why correlation alone does not establish causation.
questions.a: It identifies a relationship but does not by itself prove causation
wrong: A positive correlation always proves causation
Any relationship automatically rules out other explanations

questions.q: Define causal claim in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A claim that changing one factor produces a change in another
wrong: A statement that two variables are associated without a cause
A statement that every result is perfectly accurate

questions.q: Name the term for “a claim that changing one factor produces a change in another”.
questions.a: causal claim
wrong: correlation
measurement precision

questions.q: Explain why a claim of causation needs evidence from a valid controlled investigation.
questions.a: It requires a valid controlled investigation rather than correlation alone
wrong: Correlation alone is always sufficient proof
A single uncontrolled observation proves the cause

questions.q: Define outlier in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A data point far from the overall pattern
wrong: A data point lying exactly on the overall trend
The mean of all results

questions.q: Name the term for “a data point far from the overall pattern”.
questions.a: outlier
wrong: line of best fit
controlled condition

questions.q: Explain why excluding an outlier must be scientifically justified.
questions.a: Its cause should be investigated and any exclusion justified
wrong: Every outlier must be deleted immediately
Only results matching the prediction should be kept

questions.q: Define risk matrix in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A way of comparing likelihood and severity to judge risk level
wrong: A table showing only the costs of equipment
A graph of the measured dependent variable

questions.q: Name the term for “a way of comparing likelihood and severity to judge risk level”.
questions.a: risk matrix
wrong: results table
scatter graph

questions.q: Explain why risk matrix matters in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: It helps prioritise the hazards that need the strongest controls
wrong: It guarantees no accidents can occur
It replaces all practical safety controls

questions.q: Define method evaluation in a scientific investigation.
questions.a: A reasoned judgement about strengths, limitations and improvements
wrong: A list of results with no judgement
A repetition of the hypothesis without considering evidence

questions.q: Name the term for “a reasoned judgement about strengths, limitations and improvements”.
questions.a: method evaluation
wrong: directional hypothesis
method instructions

questions.q: State what an evaluation of an investigation should explain about weaknesses and improvements.
questions.a: It links each limitation to its likely effect on the evidence
wrong: Only whether the expected result was obtained
Only the names of equipment, with no effect on evidence
